newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end higher before U.S. attack on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end higher before U.S. attack on Iraq.

text.p: Tokyo stocks swung back to positive territory by the close on Tuesday, but the market did not have an opportunity to react to news that the United States had launched a missile attack against Iraq, brokers said.
The Nikkei had briefly slipped to below 20,000 at the open.
The morning drop stimulated buying after four consecutive days of declines, they said.
The key 225-share Nikkei average closed up 91.04 points or 0.45 percent at 20,198.15. It dropped to as low as 19,920.02 in the early morning. Its September futures gained 100 points to end at 20,250.

Minutes before the Tokyo stock market closed, the Pentagon said the U.S. military had launched cruise missile strikes against air defense targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds.

"The market could not digest the news before the close," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager at Nomura Securities Co Ltd. "We have to wait for further developments and its impact on Wall Street."
He added that if the U.S.-Iraq conflict widens and triggers a battle in the Middle East, it could hurt U.S. stocks and dampen Japanese stocks as well.

The key Nikkei average had breached the psychologically important 20,000 level right after the opening mainly because the market was disappointed at the growing possibility of a delay in a government supplementary budget, brokers said.
"The market was depressed by the government's negative attitude towards the formation of a supplementary budget," Higashida said.
"But the break through below 20,000 provided a good buying opportunity for investors," he said.
But analysts also said that the market's recovery was feeble amid the light trading volume.
Kenzo Doi, senior analyst at Kokusai Securities Co Ltd, said the Nikkei average had hit a temporary bottom as the market lacked energy, with trading volume remaining slim.
Turnover was about 264 million shares on Tuesday, compared with Monday's 203 million shares.
The market has been hurt by a grim outlook for the domestic economy since the Bank of Japan's tankan corporate survey last week showed unexpectedly weak business sentiment.
"If the government does not form a supplementary budget, this could in turn disappoint the market and send stock prices lower," Doi said.
Speculation that the government might be reluctant to announce a supplementary budget was heightened by a report by the influential Nihon Keizai Shimbun financial paper that mentioned further delays.

Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said that he had met with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and the two agreed to look at overall economic conditions in the first half of calendar 1996 before making a final decision on a supplementary budget.
In other indices of Japanese stocks, the TOPIX index of all first section stocks gained 6.45 points or 0.42 percent to end at 1,546.12.
The Nikkei 300 average gained 0.81 points or 0.28 percent to close at 287.85.
Advancing issues outpaced decliners 713 to 332, while 178 issues were unchanged.
Gainers were led by railway/bus, iron/steel, securities, communications and fisheries. The key retreating sectors were pulp/paper, warehouses and land transport.
The second section index added 1.13 points to 2,114.77, with 7.48 million shares traded. The over-the-counter (OTC) index lost 4.70 points to finish at 1,564.98.
-- Hiroko Nakata, Tokyo Equities Desk (81-3-3432-8027)
